docs.title: Strata
docs.text:
Strata is a design for a systems language that keeps Rust's memory safety and Goose's compiler-managed arenas, and asks the programmer for far less ceremony. It aims at servers: many cheap virtual threads, shared caches, deterministic cleanup, and no lifetime annotations.

Status

Exploratory. There is no compiler yet. The .stra files in the repository are Strata as it would be written, and the C beside them is what a compiler would emit, written by hand and kept honest by tests and benchmarks.

docs.title: The design in six lines
docs.text:
1. Ordinary values carry no reference-count header; new makes a strong Ref<T>, and WeakRef<T> breaks cycles.
  2. Lifetimes are inferred, not written.
  3. Shared state is accessed through sync (read) and mutate (write) blocks; entering one may park the virtual thread.
  4. Nothing is hidden except virtual threads and parking: no implicit buffering, batching or retry.
  5. Every unbounded input has a declared limit, enforced before the data is held.
  6. Errors are exceptions declared with throws; cleanup never parks and never throws.

The full text is strata-design.md.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Rules the design has settled on, with the reason each was chosen.

Decision Why Nothing hidden except virtual threads and parking Programs stay predictable; batching and buffering must be asked for. Every unbounded input has a declared limit Memory is bounded before data is held; big bodies are streamed or spooled. No biased reference counting in v1 Equal or worse once objects cross threads; confined types get plain counts. Per-type arenas, no compaction Segregates lifetimes; addresses stay stable, which the lock order relies on. Chunk epochs in resident chunk headers MADV_DONTNEED zero-fills decommitted generation words. MADV_NOHUGEPAGE on stack pools With transparent huge pages a 64 KB stack costs 65 KB resident. Errors are exceptions with throws Throwing is visible in signatures; no throws clause means nothing escapes. Cleanup never parks and never throws It runs on every exit path, including unwinding. sync/mutate acquisition parks, FIFO Fairness, and workers keep running other vthreads. Spin briefly before parking Pure parking lost up to 75% of throughput under mixed load. Multi-object heads acquire all-or-nothing Mis-ordered heads cannot deadlock. Default slow-subscriber policy: Disconnect Never silently loses messages; Notice is available. Not yet confirmed by the user. Strata identifiers are camelCase User preference. Constants stay UPPER_CASE; generated C may use underscores. Syntax: T?, methods in types, optional self, Pattern -> {} arms Avoids Rust-isms. No third-party crates in converted programs Strata would have no equivalents. Performance goal: same class as Rust async and Java vthreads, with a simpler model Superiority is not claimed; ceremony is measured alongside speed. Programming model (vthreads) is separate from implementation (resumable frames) No feature may depend on the implementation; stackful runtime kept as reference. Compiler inserts slice checks only in functions marked [yield] (or in a type or package marked so, innermost wins); [noyield] overrides; [nopark] asserts no parking at all Principle 10: nothing is inserted unless the code says so. Loops add no effect by default, so looping helpers are usable under locks without tagging. The cost is that unmarked CPU-bound code can stall a worker, which warnings aim to find. Loop warnings are a lint with an advisory loops class in the module summary, off by default except unbounded loops in lock bodies Termination is undecidable; the class is kept out of the contract hash so loop changes never force rebuilds. One Ref<T>; sharing is inferred, not declared. sync/mutate required where the object is not provably local and the field is mutable; no-ops on unshared objects Programmer never decides what is shared; a missing or too-weak block is a compile error; layout and behaviour do not depend on other modules. Cost of per-instance flag still to measure. Java folder convention: a package is a folder, every file declares package path.to.folder, a package compiles to one .smod, imports name packages, and the package default attribute is repeated on the package line of every file (no special file) A unit for module compilation, visibility and the [yield]/[noyield]/[nopark] default. The details are open (D14). C stays the backend Under the module architecture too. Strata source and C live in separate folders stra/ is Strata only; c/ is runtime and compiler-output stand-ins.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Per-instance sharing: does the flag test on each reference-count operation cost more than always-atomic for non-local references? See sharing.
  • Sharing (direction chosen, see sharing): the cost of the per-instance shared flag, publishing a graph, where the lock word lives, write-once fields across modules, access modes on interfaces.
  • When does a growable array get a dedicated virtual region instead of a relocatable buffer?
  • Exact string representation, slicing and UTF-8 indexing.
  • How does a throw interact with a scope that still has child vthreads?
  • Stack model: fixed reserve with guard pages, or segmented stacks.
  • How are exported lifetime and effect metadata versioned? Direction in architecture; policy open.
  • Architecture decisions D1 to D14 (D14: packages and imports) (where lowering happens, borrowed locals with lazy frames, minimum IR, effects in public interfaces, fusion across modules, debugging maps, dynamic loading, blocking FFI, slice-check overhead and loop warnings): open decisions.

docs.title: Sharing and access checking
docs.text:
One reference kind, Ref<T>. Whether an object is shared is not written anywhere. The compiler works out where a sync or mutate block is required, reports a missing or too-weak one as a compile error, and the blocks cost almost nothing on an object that was never shared. All examples are taken or adapted from stra/redis/db.stra.

Status: Direction. Replaces the open questions about "how shareability is proven or declared" (spec 10.2, 10.3, 7.3). Nothing here is implemented; the C beside the .stra is hand-written.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
R1. When is a block required? Reading or writing through a Ref<T> (or a borrow derived from it) needs a block naming that reference when both hold:

  1. the object is not provably local, and
  2. the accessed field, or anything stored by value inside it, is mutable.

R2. Provably local. The object was allocated in this function with new, and no reference to it has escaped so far on any path: it has not been passed to a function whose summary says it retains or publishes the argument, stored into a non-local object, captured by a closure, or given to spawn or a message. Everything else is incoming: a parameter, a global, a field of a non-local object, or a call result not marked fresh (below).

R3. Mutable. A field is mutable if anything outside object construction writes it, directly or through a method whose access summary says it writes its receiver (entries.insert(...) mutates entries). A field never written after construction is write-once, and reading it needs no block. A type whose fields are all write-once is immutable, and it needs no block anywhere.

R4. Modes. sync is read-only; mutate is exclusive. Writing needs mutate. A call made inside sync to a function whose summary writes the argument is an error: needs mutate(store), have sync(store). This is checked even for an object that turns out never to be shared, so behaviour does not depend on sharing.

R5. Publishing. A reference to a local object crosses a vthread boundary when it is passed to spawn, sent in a message, stored in a global or in a non-local object, or captured by a closure that is. From that point the object is shared: the compiler treats the reference as no longer local on every later path, so R1 applies after it. At run time the object's shared flag is set before the handoff, and everything reachable from it is set too (or the compiler refuses the publish; see Open).

R6. Cost on an unshared object. sync/mutate test the flag once at entry. If it is clear, they do nothing. The flag only ever goes from clear to set, so the test at exit agrees with the one at entry.

R7. Borrows. A borrow taken inside a block cannot leave it (return, store, capture). A T& parameter needs no block in the callee: the caller either owns the object locally or holds the block (R4 checks its mode against the callee's summary).

R8. Runtime types. A type declared extern (Signal, Flag, Limiter, Mailbox, Wakeup) synchronises itself. Its methods need no block, whoever calls them and whether or not the object is shared; the extern declaration is a promise, as it is for parking. Only Strata-defined types follow R1 to R7.

Fresh results. A function whose result is a new allocation that nothing else refers to is marked fresh in its summary, so let db = Db.make(lim) is local in the caller until it escapes. Without fresh the caller must treat the result as incoming.

Mutability, escape (retains/publishes), access mode per parameter, and fresh are Tier A contract data (modules). Changing a field from write-once to mutable is a breaking change.

docs.title: Example 1: local use, no blocks
docs.text:
A test or a command-line tool builds a store and reads it back in one vthread. Nothing escapes, so there is nothing to lock.

// tools/load.stra
package tools

fn loadAndCount(path: string&): usize {
    let store = new Store {}              // local
    for line in readLines(path) {
        store.entries.insert(Bytes.copyOf(line.key), Entry { value: new Value { bytes: line.value.copy() }, expiresAt: null })
    }
    return store.entries.count            // local: no sync, no mutate
}

Under the earlier SharedRef idea this would have needed a different type or a separate shared variant. Here it is the same Store and the same code as the server uses.

docs.title: Example 2: what Db needs and what it does not
docs.text:
// redis/db.stra
package redis

struct Db {                               // every field is set in make() and never written again: write-once
    store: Ref<Store>
    purgeWake: Signal
    closed: Flag
    reaper: Ref<Mailbox<Reap>>
    lim: Limits
    // ...
    fn get(key: u8[]&): Ref<Value>? {
        sync(store) {                     // R1: store is incoming and Store.entries is mutable
            let e = store.entries.get(key)
            return e == null ? null : e.value
        }
    }

    fn[nopark] release(channel: u8[]&, mb: Ref<Mailbox<Message>>) {
        reaper.tryPush(Reap { ... })      // reaper is write-once and Mailbox is an extern handle (R8): no block; [nopark] lets cleanup() call it
    }
}
stra/redis/db.stra is written this way, with these notes in its header.

  • db.store and db.lim are read with no block, because those fields never change after make. This is why the existing code already writes sync(store) and not sync(db).
  • store.entries is mutated by set, purgeExpired and others, so reads and writes of it go through sync/mutate.
  • Value is "immutable once built". After get returns the Ref<Value> the caller reads v.bytes with no block, which is exactly what the comment in db.stra relies on when it writes the reply after the lock is released.

docs.title: Example 3: errors the compiler reports
docs.text:
// redis/stats.stra
package redis

fn size(db: Db&): usize {
    return db.store.entries.count         // error: store.entries is mutable and db is incoming
}                                         //   fix: sync(db.store) { return db.store.entries.count }

// redis/trim.stra
package redis

fn trim(store: Ref<Store>) {
    sync(store) {
        store.entries.remove(oldest(store))   // error: entries.remove writes its receiver
    }                                         //   needs mutate(store), have sync(store)
}

// redis/peek.stra
package redis

fn peekKeys(store: Ref<Store>): Map<Bytes, Entry>& {
    sync(store) {
        return store.entries              // error: a borrow taken in a sync block cannot leave it
    }
}

The messages name the chain and the fix. A missing block on a reference that turns out never to be shared is still reported: that is the over-approximation in R2, and the cost is one extra block that does nothing at run time.

docs.title: Example 4: publishing, and what changes after it
docs.text:
// redis/main.stra
package redis

fn main(args: Args&) {
    let db = Db.make(lim)                 // fresh: local so far
    db.purgeWake.notify()                 // Signal is a runtime handle, not db's mutable state
    spawn db.purgeLoop()                  // R5: db is published here
    let n = db.store.entries.count        // error: db is shared from the spawn on; entries is mutable
    serve(listener, db, lim, shutdown, live)
}

Before the spawn, db is local and could be inspected directly. After it, every access to mutable state follows R1. Moving the line above the spawn makes it legal, and correct, since no other vthread yet exists.

docs.title: Example 5: modes across a call
docs.text:
// redis/expire.stra
package redis

fn expireAndCount(store: Ref<Store>): usize {
    mutate(store) {
        purgeBatch(store)                 // summary: purgeBatch writes param 0 -> mutate required: ok
        return store.entries.count
    }
}

fn statsOnly(store: Ref<Store>): usize {
    sync(store) {
        purgeBatch(store)                 // error: purgeBatch writes its argument; have sync(store)
        return store.entries.count
    }
}

The check uses purgeBatch's summary, so it works when purgeBatch is in another module and its source is not available.

docs.title: What the module file carries
docs.text:
Db.get      self.store: read via sync, result: not fresh, throws: none, park: May
Db.make     result: fresh, retains lim
Store       entries: mutable   expirations: mutable   topics: mutable
Value       bytes: write-once  (type is immutable)
Db          store, purgeWake, closed, reaper, lim: write-once
purgeBatch  param 0: write

A consumer of db.smod can run every check above with no source. An implementation change that makes Db.lim mutable changes the contract hash and is reported as a breaking change, because every reader of lim now needs a block.

docs.title: Generated C for a block
docs.text:
// sync(store) { ... } where store is incoming
bool sh = obj_is_shared(store);                  // one load of the control-block flag
if (sh) { st_t s = rwlock_read_enter(t, &store->lock); /* may park; PARKED unwinds as usual */ }
/* body: no parking inside, no slice checks */
if (sh) rwlock_read_exit(&store->lock);          // on every exit path, including throws

Reference counts follow the same split. An object the compiler proves local uses plain counts. A reference to a non-local object tests the flag: plain count if clear, atomic if set. That test per copy and release is a real cost, and the alternative (always atomic for non-local) is simpler and slower; bench/c/refcount_bench.c is where it gets measured (Open).

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• Publishing a graph. Setting the flag on everything reachable costs a walk at the publish. Alternatives: refuse to publish an object whose graph has local-only parts that are not themselves being published; or make spawn and message sends take only values whose reachable graph is already shared or immutable.
  • Where the lock word lives. In every control block (costs bytes on every new), or allocated at the first publish (costs an indirection).
  • Counts per instance. A flag test in each count operation, or atomic always for non-local references. Needs refcount_bench on realistic access patterns.
  • Write-once across modules. A field is write-once if no code in its defining module writes it. Public fields that other modules may write need either a mutability declaration or a rule that they are mutable by default.
  • Immutable types. Inferred from R3 as above; whether to also let the programmer assert it (for a compile error if a later change breaks it) is undecided.
  • Runtime types that are not thread-safe. R8 treats every extern type as self-synchronising. Whether an extern declaration may say otherwise (a handle that one vthread must own) is undecided.
  • Interfaces and function values. A call through one needs a declared access mode per parameter, as it needs an effect bound. Default is "writes", the safe direction for the caller.
  • Lint. A value read in a sync block and used to decide a write in a separate mutate block on the same object (the get-then-put race of spec 7.2). A warning, not an error.

docs.title: Architecture: compilation, suspension and modules
docs.text:
This section extends strata-design.md (sections 5, 6 and 14). It is a design update, not an implementation plan for the compiler to start tomorrow. There is still no compiler: the C in c/ is hand-written to look like compiler output.

Page Covers This page Objective, the two models, the pipeline, what happens where Suspension and continuations The may-park effect, resumable frames, recursion, cancellation, cleanup, fusion Compiled modules and linking The module format, the three information tiers, ABI and IR boundaries, incremental versus optimised builds, recompilation rules Dynamic dispatch and external code Interfaces, function values, generics, C interop, blocking foreign calls, callbacks, dynamic loading Evaluation plan How Strata is compared with Java virtual threads and Rust async Open decisions Unresolved questions, alternatives, recommended direction Changes and contradictions What this update changed in the existing design, and what it contradicted

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: The target is excellent performance with a simpler programming model, not performance superiority. A Strata server should be written as plain sequential code (no async/await, no lifetime names, no pinning, no executor choice) and should land in the same performance class as hand-tuned Rust async or Java virtual-thread code. When the two disagree, the simpler source wins, provided the cost is measured and stated. The evaluation plan therefore measures source ceremony as well as speed.

docs.title: Status labels
docs.text:
Every claim on these pages carries one of four statuses, so that speculation is not read as decision.

Label Meaning Decided Already settled in docs/decisions.md or the specification. Direction The recommended choice. Reasoned but not validated by a compiler. Open Alternatives are listed; no recommendation is binding yet. Measured Backed by a result in bench/results/. These are hand-written C, so they bound what a compiler could achieve; they do not show that one does.

docs.title: Two models, kept apart
docs.text:
Programming model (Decided). Virtual threads. A vthread runs ordinary sequential code; a call that may wait looks like any other call. The programmer sees stackful-like semantics: locals live across a wait, a try spans it, cleanup runs when scopes exit, and a cancelled task unwinds.

Implementation model (Direction). Compiler-generated resumable frames, which are stackless continuations. The compiler finds the calls that may park, gives each function that can suspend a frame holding exactly the state live across its suspension points, and generates a state machine. There is no per-vthread machine stack.

Nothing in the language may depend on which implementation is used. A program that behaves correctly under stackful fibers must behave identically under resumable frames. That is the test for any proposed feature, and it is why the existing stackful runtime stays useful as a reference (see suspension).

"Park" and "suspend" mean the same thing. The specification and the C runtime say park, so this section does too, and calls the inferred property the may-park effect.

docs.title: What happens where
docs.text:
Step Module compile Application link Notes Parse, type check, borrow and effect inference within the module Yes Needs only the module and the interfaces it imports Typed IR and module file Yes Lower every function to the Level-0 calling convention Yes (Direction) Makes a module linkable with no IR from anyone else Check imported contract hashes Yes Also at module compile, against the interface used Whole-program effect resolution (conditional effects, interface calls) Yes Cheap; works on summaries, not IR Devirtualise where the implementation set is closed Optimised mode Needs retained IR only if the target is then inlined Cross-module inlining and frame fusion Optimised mode Needs retained IR Lowering of fused or embedded frames Optimised mode Output replaces the module-level code for the chains it touches C compile and link Per module (cached) Once

Whether module compilation lowers fully, or lowering waits for the link, is open. The recommendation is both: lower at module compile so a build with no optimisation never needs the retained IR, and re-lower only what fusion changes.

A minor source change must not mean a whole-program rebuild. The rules that guarantee this are in recompilation rules.

docs.title: Evaluation plan
docs.text: The question is not "is Strata faster?" It is: does Strata reach the same performance class as Java virtual threads and Rust async, with a measurably simpler program? Both halves are measured. A result that is slightly slower with much less source ceremony is a success; a result that is faster with a more complicated model is not the goal.

docs.title: What exists, and what it does not show
docs.text: The HTTP, mini-redis and micro benchmarks in bench/ are promising (see docs/journey/ and bench/results/). They are hand-written C beside hand-written Rust/Go/Java. They do not show that a compiler can generate the same code, and the simple HTTP handler is syscall-bound at roughly 3 microseconds a request, so throughput there is nearly equal by construction. They are not representative of applications with deep call chains, databases, TLS, dispatch or cancellation. Treat them as evidence about the runtime, nothing more.

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
1. Equivalent behaviour. Same protocol, same limits, same error behaviour, same cleanup, on the same wire. Each variant passes the same black-box test suite before it is timed (the existing run_tests.sh pattern).
  2. Comparable I/O models. Strata (readiness plus epoll) against Tokio (epoll) and Java virtual threads on the JDK's NIO selector. Not against blocking thread-per-request unless that is the stated question.
  3. Idiomatic baselines. The Rust and Java versions are written by someone who would ship them, with the executor and pool settings tuned and recorded.
  4. Pre-registered bars. Before measuring, write down what counts as "same class" (for example, within a stated factor on throughput and p99 latency, and no worse on memory). The factor is set once and not adjusted afterwards. No factor is proposed here; it is a decision for the author once the first end-to-end numbers exist.
  5. Report variance. Repeated runs, pinned CPUs, fixed frequency, warm-up for the JVM, p50/p99/p99.9, not only means.
  6. Scheduler cost is separated from application cost. Each workload is run with a null body (spawn, park, resume, finish) to get the pure scheduling and frame overhead, and with the real body. Reported as: total = scheduling + application.
  7. Nothing is claimed beyond what ran. A benchmark that has no Strata compiler behind it is labelled hand-written.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text:
# Workload What it tests Notes B1 Minimal HTTP handler Floor cost; allocation per request Exists (bench/http). Syscall-bound. B2 Deep call chain, park at depth 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 Frame creation, direct-resume benefit, effect inference Extends frames_bench and lazy_bench. Generate chains with a compiler when one exists. B3 Sequential I/O: N dependent reads Wake cost, scheduler fairness B4 Concurrent I/O: fan-out and join Child vthreads, structured scopes B5 Database pool and queries Pool wait as park, parked-frame memory, real wire protocol Same database, same schema, same driver protocol. B6 Outbound HTTP and TLS Native C interop; blocking vs nonblocking foreign calls TLS library choice affects all variants; record it. B7 Dynamic dispatch May bound on a hot interface call, status test, thunks Include devirtualised and non-devirtualised builds. B8 Cancellation, timeouts and errors Unwinding through frames, cleanup timing, leaked resources Correctness first: every cleanup ran exactly once. Then latency of cancellation. B9 Very many vthreads 100k to 1M idle and mostly-idle tasks, memory per task Extends the existing fiber/frames tables. B10 Memory and allocation Resident and virtual bytes, allocations per request, frame arena fragmentation Report RSS and VSZ separately; run under THP on and off (a known trap in this project). B11 Blocking FFI Offload pool: latency of the thread hop, behaviour when the pool is full Compare strategies 2 and 4 of dispatch. B13 Slice-check overhead Tight loops (hashing, parsing, copying, brc-style scans) as plain C, with [yield] checks, and with strip-mined checks; time to yield and fairness under a CPU-bound task The cost of opting in. Also decides whether default-on is ever worth revisiting. B12 Mixed realistic service Parse, route, query, render, with a shared cache (sync/mutate) The end-to-end result everything else supports.

Metrics for all: throughput, CPU utilisation (user, system), p50/p99/p99.9 latency, resident memory, allocations, context switches.

docs.title: Ceremony metrics (the half that matters most here)
docs.text:
For each application, written equivalently in Strata, Rust and Java:

  • Lines of code and number of tokens.
  • Count of async/await, Pin, Box<dyn ...>, lifetime names, Arc/Mutex wrapper types, executor/runtime setup lines.
  • Count of explicit cancellation or resource-handling constructs.
  • Whether a reviewer who has not seen the code can state where it may wait (needs tooling support for Strata; its quality is part of the result).

The Rust and Java versions are not made artificially verbose; the comparison is only meaningful for code each community would write.

docs.title: Build and tooling measurements
docs.text:
Because the module architecture trades build time for runtime, these are measured as results, not assumed:

  • Clean build; incremental rebuild after (a) a body change that keeps the contract, (b) a contract-changing change, (c) an effect-widening change at depth. Report modules recompiled and wall-clock.
  • Optimised link time against application size; with and without cached products.
  • Module file size by tier (A, B, C) for a representative library.
  • Whether the output of optimised mode beats incremental mode by an amount that justifies it. If it does not, that finding stands.

docs.title: What this update changed
docs.text:
Area Before Now Virtual-thread implementation Spec 6.1: stackful fibers with independently managed stacks Programming model unchanged; implementation is compiler-generated resumable frames (Direction). Stackful runtime kept as reference and baseline Parking Spec principle 10, leaves.stra: inferred may-park effect, informally Defined as a lattice (Never, Cond(P), May) with propagation rules, exported in contracts Separate compilation Spec 5.1: interface artifact with borrow origins and effects A full module format with three information tiers, hashes, versions and a native-cache key Compiler architecture Not described (Phase 0 and 5 only) The pipeline in index; C stays the backend Interfaces, function values, FFI Spec 5.2, 9, 10.9 mention them Bound-based dispatch, extern blocking, callbacks, dynamic loading rules Evaluation Spec Phase 6: "against Tokio or Java vthreads" A workload set, ground rules, ceremony metrics, build metrics Sharing Undecided: shared var, shareable Ref<T>, or a type-level declaration One Ref<T>; sharing inferred; blocks required by path analysis (sharing) Open questions 10.8 stacks, 10.10 API stability Superseded and refined into D1 to D14

The syntax of existing Strata is unchanged. Proposed additions, each marked placeholder and Open: the package declaration (placeholder), the attributes [yield], [noyield] and [nopark] (control of compiler-inserted slice checks and an assertion of no parking), and extern blocking.

docs.title: Contradictions found, and how each is resolved
docs.text:
1. Stackful fibers vs resumable frames. Spec 6.1 said stackful; the C runtime (c/runtime/rt.h) and frames_bench use sized frames; ASSESSMENT.md flagged this. Resolved: frames are the implementation direction; 6.1 is rewritten; the stackful runtime is demoted to reference and baseline. The frame/idle-memory numbers are labelled hand-written and are not evidence about generated code.
  2. Stack-size questions. Spec 10.8 (fixed reserve vs segmented stacks) assumed stackful. Resolved: applies only to the stackful baseline and the native stack used by fast paths; the 4 KB floor and guard-page findings remain valid for that baseline.
  3. "Lifetime contracts are compile-time only" vs executables needing effect info. Spec 5.1 says metadata is a compile-time dependency and the executable need not contain it. Still true for Tier A; but park-point tables (debug) and Level-0 entry names are in the executable if tooling is wanted. Resolved: debug sections are optional and separable.
  4. Borrow across a park vs the lazy frame strategy. The lazy measurements assumed no borrowed locals. Flagged: D2.
  5. "No hidden behaviour" vs inferred effects ripple. An implementation change can now change a contract. Flagged, partly resolved: the exception in principle 10 is extended to effect contracts, mitigated by contract diffs, optional assertions and a version policy (D4).
  6. Cooperative cancellation and scheduling vs tasks that never park. Previously a limitation. Resolved by decision: the compiler inserts slice checks only in functions marked [yield] (or a type, later a package, marked so), which makes those loops yield and cancellation points. Unmarked CPU-bound code can still stall a worker; warnings, a watchdog and the type-level default address it. Remaining gaps and the overhead question are in D13.
  7. Foreign callbacks vs vthreads. A callback cannot be suspended. Resolved by the Never default and the synchronous driver on pool threads.

docs.title: Outstanding decisions
docs.text:
Short list; reasoning in open decisions.

D1 where lowering happens; D2 borrowed locals; D3 minimum IR; D4 effects in public interfaces; D5 recursion and dispatch limits; D6 generics; D7 fusion across modules; D8 debugging and profiling; D9 dynamic loading; D10 blocking FFI; D11 compatibility policy and caches; D12 cancellation semantics; D13 slice-check overhead and unit (mechanism decided: opt-in [yield]); D14 packages and imports.

docs.text:
• Any compiler output. All Level-0 C is illustrative or hand-written.
  • Exceptions as status returns in generated C.
  • Build-time and module-size costs.
  • The frequency of borrowed-across-park locals in real handlers.

docs.title: Dynamic dispatch and external code
docs.text: Rule for everything on this page: a call whose target cannot be fixed at compile time is compiled against a declared bound, never against what the implementation happens to do today. Later releases of an implementation may then change freely inside the bound, and a program that compiled keeps being valid.

docs.title: Interface calls
docs.text:
An interface method has a declared effect bound: the widest effect any implementation may have.

  • Default bound: May (Direction). Safe, and cheap because a May call that does not park costs about a call plus a status test (Measured, toy). A bound is written only when the author wants to narrow it, using the same [nopark] attribute as for functions (placeholder syntax; D4).
  • Implementations are checked against the bound when they are compiled. An implementation can be narrower than the bound, never wider. An implementation of a nopark method that calls a May function is a compile error in the implementing module.
  • Callers compile the call against the bound. A caller of a May-bound method uses the suspendable form regardless of the implementation.
  • Vtable entries for May methods hold the f_call/f_resume pair. An implementation that is Never registers a thunk that returns DONE, so the calling code is the same.
  • At link time, if the closed-world call graph shows one reachable implementation, the call may be devirtualised and the thunk and the status test removed. If several implementations exist, the bound still holds; any narrowing is an optimisation of the call site (a switch over known targets), never a change of contract.

This is the answer to "previously valid programs becoming unsafe when implementations change": the check that matters happens in the implementing module against a bound the caller already relied on.

docs.title: Function values and callbacks
docs.text:
A function-typed value (fn(u8[]&): Resp throws Exception) carries a bound the same way. Unannotated, it is May. A value that can be shown Never at the point where it is created (a lambda with no parking calls) can be passed where a May bound is expected. The reverse needs the assertion.

Functions that take function-typed parameters have a conditional summary Cond(P): forEach(list, f) parks iff f may. At a call site where f is statically known, the condition collapses and the call binds to the plain or the suspendable form. At one where it is not, the parameter's declared bound is used.

Callbacks that the runtime invokes (a handler, a timer) are May by contract; the runtime calls the f_call/f_resume pair.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
Direction: monomorphise (one copy per type argument set, as in C++ and Rust), because it gives each instance exact frame layouts and an exact effect. It needs Tier B IR from the defining module, and instances land in the using module's object (or a link-time instance cache).

A generic function's summary is symbolic in the type arguments: Cond({T}) if it calls a method of T, whose bound comes from the constraint. Resolved at instantiation. The generic body's IR is part of its contract hash, so editing a generic body forces dependants that instantiate it to recompile.

Open (D6): shared generic code with a dictionary, which avoids code growth and makes generics independent of IR retention but costs speed and requires uniform frame layouts for generic locals.

docs.title: Separately compiled libraries
docs.text:
Libraries are compiled modules. Their interfaces are Tier A. The rules in modules cover: contract hash checks at link; widening an effect or layout is breaking; implementations behind interfaces change freely within the bound.

A library that is only available as a native object and header (no .smod) is a foreign library and takes the rules below.

docs.title: Native C interoperability
docs.text:
C declarations carry no ownership or effect information (spec 5.2). A Strata binding must state it:

// bindings/crc.stra
package bindings

extern fn crc32(data: u8[]&): u32                  // plain: Never. Assumed short and non-blocking.
extern parks fn sleep(d: Duration)                   // existing: a runtime primitive that registers and parks
extern blocking fn pqExec(c: PgConn&, sql: string&) // proposed: may block the OS thread (see below)

An extern fn without a modifier is a promise that it returns quickly and does not block. The compiler cannot verify the promise and nothing in the runtime enforces it. A violation stalls one worker for the length of the call (the same failure mode as a Java thread stuck while pinned); a watchdog may report it (see the table).

extern blocking is the one proposed new keyword in this update (Open; placeholder). It states that the call may block the thread, and is the only way a binding can say so. It carries foreign = blocking and park = May in the summary: the Strata caller sees an ordinary suspending call.

docs.title: Blocking foreign calls
docs.text:
A foreign C function is native stack that cannot be captured, so it cannot be suspended in the middle. Strategies, in order of preference:

Strategy What happens Cost and limits 1. Nonblocking binding (best) Use a readiness/async API of the library (nonblocking sockets, epoll, io_uring); the Strata wrapper calls it and parks on the descriptor. Library must offer it. No extra thread. 2. Offload to a blocking pool (Direction for extern blocking) The call is a park point: the vthread parks, a pool thread runs the call, and a completion wakes the vthread. A thread hop per call (some microseconds); a bounded pool, so a full pool queues work (and that wait is itself a park). Arguments must outlive the park: borrowed arguments must be frame-resident, not on the native stack (same rule as here). Thread-affine libraries need a pinned thread (strategy 3). 3. Dedicated thread A thread owns a library (a connection, a context) and Strata sends it work and awaits replies as messages. Serialises that library's calls; good for thread-affine code. 4. Run on the worker Plain extern fn: the call blocks the worker. Only right for calls that are truly short. Stalls everything on that worker. 5. Compensating worker A monitor notices a worker stuck in foreign code past a threshold and starts another worker so the scheduler keeps a core busy. Does not fix the stuck call. Useful as a backstop and as a diagnostic, not a design.

Recommendation: 1 where available, 2 as the default for anything declared extern blocking, 3 for thread-affine libraries, and a watchdog (diagnostic only, 5's detection without its remedy) for promises broken under 4. All are Open until measured: cost of the thread hop is exactly the kind of figure the evaluation plan must record.

docs.title: Foreign callbacks
docs.text:
C code calls a Strata function (a qsort comparator, a library event callback). The callback runs on whatever native stack C is using.

  • Default (Direction): a callback is compiled as Never (it may call only Never functions, and no slice check is inserted). Calling a May function from it is a compile error. Because a callback is invoked from C, it is f_call-only: nothing underneath it can be captured.
  • Exception: callbacks that must park. Declared as parking callbacks, they run on a blocking-pool thread only, under a synchronous driver: the wrapper calls f_call; on PARKED it blocks the OS thread on a wake-up object, and on the wake calls f_resume until DONE. Parking then blocks that thread, not a scheduler worker. This is the block_on of Strata. It is forbidden on scheduler workers (compile error if the call is made from a worker context that is not a pool thread; at minimum, a runtime check).
  • Exceptions cannot cross a C frame. The wrapper catches THROWN and converts it to the library's error convention or aborts. The binding says which.

docs.title: Dynamically loaded modules
docs.text:
Direction: not supported in the first compiler. It must stay possible, so the contract design assumes it:

  • A loadable module is a native shared object plus its .smod interface. At load, the runtime checks: format and ABI versions, imported contract hashes against what is already loaded, and that any interface implementations it registers satisfy the declared bounds.
  • A loaded module can be Never, Cond or May per function like any other; its callers are compiled against bounds, so no reanalysis is needed. This is the benefit of bound-based dispatch.
  • Tension with whole-program optimisation: devirtualisation and fusion assume the set of implementations is closed. A plugin can add implementations. The application's build configuration therefore names the open interfaces (those plugins may implement); calls through them are never devirtualised and keep the thunks. Everything else stays closed-world. The configuration, not new source syntax, carries this (Open, D9).
  • Unloading is out of scope: frames and vtables may point into a module.

docs.title: Compiled modules and application linking
docs.text: A compiled Strata module (working extension .smod; a bundle of them is an archive, .sar) is the compiled form of one source package (a folder of files that all start with the same package name line, see D14); the module takes the package's name. It is what a library ships and what an application consumes. It carries enough to type-check, lifetime-check, effect-check and optimise a program against it without the original source. Names and extensions are placeholders.

docs.title: 1. Three tiers of information
docs.text:
The module separates what is needed for correctness from what only enables optimisation. A consumer can drop a higher tier and still get a correct program.

Tier Purpose Contents If absent A: Contract Correctness Exported types and layouts, signatures, borrow origins, effect summaries, interface/dispatch contracts, generic constraints, ownership metadata, versions and hashes The module cannot be used. B: Instantiation IR Correctness for generics and exposed bodies IR of generic functions and types, and of functions the author exposes for inlining Generic code cannot be instantiated downstream. (Unless generics use a shared-code representation; see D6.) C: Optimisation IR Speed and size IR of every non-generic function, call-graph edges with targets, park-point and liveness tables, frame layouts Still correct and linkable through Level-0 entries; no cross-module inlining, devirtualisation or fusion. (cache) Build speed Per-target C and native objects, keyed by hashes Rebuilt on demand.

A module can be shipped as A+B only (a "closed" library: interface and generics, plus precompiled objects) or A+B+C (an "open" one). That is the exact meaning of "without requiring the original source": the compiler needs IR, not text.

docs.title: 2. Contents of a module
docs.text:
header
  magic, format version, ABI version, compiler id
  module name, module version, target triple + layout hash
  content hash, interface hash
imports
  for each imported module: name, version range, and for each symbol used:
    the contract hash that this module was compiled against
exports                                            [Tier A]
  types: layout (or "opaque"), fields visible, cleanup method, copy/move rules,
         whether sync-able (has a lock word)
  functions: signature, per-parameter ownership mode (borrow, consume, Ref),
             borrow origins of the return value, effect summary, throws list
  interfaces: method list, per-method effect bound, vtable layout, versioning rule
  generic definitions: constraints, effect conditions (Cond(P))
  constants and static data a caller may fold
instantiation IR                                   [Tier B]
  IR for generic items and for explicitly inlinable functions
implementation                                     [Tier C]
  typed IR per function, with a per-function content hash
  call-graph edges: direct (symbol), indirect (interface method / function type + its declared bound),
                    address-taken set
  per-function park-point table: state id -> source location, live set, logical function
  frame layout (private) and the Level-0 entry names
  initialisation order and dependencies
debug (optional)
  names, line tables, logical stack maps for fused code
native cache (optional, repeatable)
  per target/compiler/flags: generated C and object, keyed by the inputs below

docs.title: Effect summaries
docs.text:
The summary is part of every exported function's contract, not an attribute of its body:

Summary(f) = {
  park:    Never | May | Cond(P)
  throws:  set of exception types that can escape
  foreign: none | nonblocking | blocking          // reaches a foreign call (see dispatch page)
  yields:  bool                                    // park=May only because of compiler-inserted slice checks ([yield]); cannot wait on I/O or a lock
}
advisory (not hashed into the contract) = {
  loops:   none | bounded | long | unbounded       // loop and recursion class of f including its callees; feeds the loop warnings
}
invariants: cleanup methods are Never; foreign=blocking implies park=May

The loops class is advisory. It records, for each exported function, the worst loop class among its own loops and those of its direct callees (nested loops compose; see suspension 1.3). It exists so a caller's lint can warn about tight -> parse -> scanForever when scanForever is in another module and its source is not available. It is stored in Tier A but kept out of the contract hash on purpose: loop structure changes often, and a change from bounded to long must not force every dependant to recompile. Consequences: a warning can lag until the caller's lint next reads the callee's current .smod, and loops is never used for code generation. Calls through interfaces, function values and foreign code are recorded as unknown contributions and not as a class.

Cond(P) is stored symbolically, so a downstream module can resolve it with its own arguments. A conditional effect through a type parameter (T.compare that might park) is stored as Cond({T}) and resolved at instantiation.

Summaries are inferred, then exported as part of the contract. The consequence, already noted for borrow origins in spec 5.1: changing an implementation can change the contract with no source signature change. The compiler reports it (versioning).

docs.title: Access and escape summaries
docs.text:
Also part of each exported function's contract, and of each exported type (see sharing):

per borrowed or Ref parameter:  access = none | read | write      (through the receiver and by-value fields)
                                escape = none | retained | published (stored beyond the call / given to spawn or a message)
result:                         fresh  = yes | no                 (a new allocation nothing else refers to)
per type field:                 mutability = write-once | mutable

These are what the compiler needs to report a missing or too-weak sync/mutate across modules without the callee's source. Changing a field from write-once to mutable, a parameter's access from read to write, or a result from fresh to not fresh is a breaking change.

docs.title: Call-graph information
docs.text:
Retained in Tier C, and also, in reduced form, in the contract:

  • Direct edges: f -> g with the symbol g (module-qualified). Enough for whole-program effect checking and for dead-code elimination.
  • Indirect edges: an interface method or function-typed value, with its declared effect bound. Resolved against known implementations at link time; never assumed resolvable.
  • Address-taken set: functions whose address escapes as a value. Needed to know which functions can be the target of a function-value call.
  • Reachability roots: exported functions, interface implementations, and initialisers.

docs.title: 3. ABI and IR boundaries
docs.text: This is the central design cut: what must stay stable for separately compiled code to link versus what is free to change.

docs.title: Level 0: the stable ABI between modules
docs.text:
Everything a caller compiled against db may rely on, and what db must keep working across releases that claim compatibility:

Item Stable? Symbol name, argument and result passing (C calling convention rules per target) Yes status values DONE/THROWN/PARKED, and the wake reasons including CANCELLED Yes The frame header (resume pointer, state number, parent link, task pointer, result binding) Yes The way a function exposes its two entries (f_call, f_resume) Yes Layout of exported types that are not opaque Yes; changing it is a breaking change Vtable layout of an interface, slot order, per-slot effect bound Yes Exception type identities Yes The frame body (live slots, state numbering, number of frames used) No. Private to the function. Whether the function uses lazy, eager or embedded frames No. The IR No. It is versioned independently; a consumer reads the IR format version.

Keeping the frame body private is what makes incremental compilation work: a caller of db.query never learns how many bytes query's frame is. A callee that changes its locals, adds a park point or switches to eager frames changes nothing a caller's object code depends on. Direction, resting on the lazy convention; if the callee's frame had to be embedded in the caller's, this would not hold (and that is why embedding happens only at link time, from IR, never at module compile).

docs.title: The IR boundary
docs.text:
The IR is what a consumer uses to regenerate code, so it must carry what the generated C needs, and no more:

  • Typed, structured control flow with ownership operations explicit: move, borrow, Ref copy and release, new, cleanup scopes, sync/mutate regions, throw edges.
  • Effects on every call site, and park points marked, so that frame lowering is a function of the IR alone.
  • Not raw source text, comments, formatting or macro structure.
  • Stable under a format version number; the consumer refuses a newer major version.

The minimum IR needed for cross-module optimisation is open (D3).

docs.title: 4. Versioning and compatibility
docs.text:
• Format version (major.minor): the layout of the file. A consumer reads any same-major file.
  • ABI version: the Level-0 rules in the table above. A different ABI means a rebuild, never a silent link.
  • Contract hash, per exported symbol: a hash of exactly its Tier A entry (and for generics and exposed bodies, the Tier B IR). It is the unit of compatibility.
  • Module interface hash: a hash of all contract hashes, for a fast check.
  • Advisory data (loops) is excluded from every hash above.
  • Compatibility rule (Direction): an implementation change that alters no contract hash is compatible. A change that narrows an effect (May to Never), reduces throws, or adds an export is backward compatible. A change that widens an effect (Never to May), adds to throws, changes layout or changes a borrow origin is breaking, whether or not the signature text changed.
  • Semantic version policy: breaking contract changes require a major version; the compiler can compare two versions of a module and print the contract diff (which symbols changed and which dimension). This answers spec 10.10 (API stability) at the tooling level; the policy itself is Open.

docs.title: The native cache key
docs.text:
A cached C or object file for a function is valid only for the inputs it was generated from:

key = hash( function IR hash,
            contract hashes of every symbol it references,
            Tier B/C IR hashes of anything inlined into it,
            module ABI + runtime ABI version,
            compiler version, C compiler id + version,
            optimisation level + codegen flags, target triple )

Any input changing gives a different key; a stale entry is never reused, only left to age out.

docs.title: Incremental compilation (default for development)
docs.text:
1. For each module, in dependency order: read the interfaces of imports (Tier A only), type-check, infer effects and borrows, produce IR, lower to Level 0, emit C, cache the object.
  2. Link the objects and the runtime with the system linker. No IR from other modules is read.
  3. Early cut-off: if a module's interface hash is unchanged after recompilation, its dependants are not touched, even though its objects changed (they relink, not recompile).

Correctness across separately compiled modules rests on Tier A plus Level 0. Calls to May functions are compiled to check status because the contract says May, whatever the body does today.

docs.title: Optimised application compilation (release builds)
docs.text:
1. Resolve all modules (names, versions, contract hashes). A mismatch between an importer's recorded hash and the provider's is an error naming the symbol.
  2. Build the closed-world call graph from Tier C edges and the build configuration (entry points, open interfaces).
  3. Check effects across modules with the summaries: a Cond(P) is resolved against real arguments; indirect calls are checked against implementations; a violated bound is an error.
  4. Re-run lifetime/borrow checks that cross modules (only the contracts are needed).
  5. Decide optimisations: devirtualise calls with a single reachable implementation, inline small functions, fuse or embed frame chains, specialise generics.
  6. Re-lower and re-emit only the functions changed by step 5. Everything else keeps its cached Level-0 object.
  7. Run the C compiler and linker; ideally with LTO as an independent layer.

Step 5 is where the retained IR is consumed. If a module lacks Tier C, calls into it stay at Level 0 and nothing else breaks.

docs.title: What each step costs
docs.text:
Cost Why Mitigation Whole-program effect resolution One pass over summaries: proportional to call-graph edges and indirect bound checks Summaries are small and cached per module; independent of code size Devirtualisation and inlining need IR Read and re-lower IR for the functions touched Limit to reachable code from roots; parallel by SCC; cache the results keyed as in section 4 Re-optimisation on change A change to one function can alter fusion decisions upstream Content-hashed products: only chains whose inlined inputs changed are regenerated IR size in the module Tier C is bigger than the contract Tier C is optional; shipped as separate section or file Cache invalidation A wrong key gives wrong code Keys include everything in section 4; unknown dimensions invalidate Cold full build Whole-program mode over all modules Not the default; development uses incremental

These costs are estimated from experience of comparable systems, not measured for Strata. Evaluating the build-time cost is part of the plan.

docs.title: 6. When a module needs recompiling
docs.text:
Recompile module M when any of these changes:

  1. M's own source (or its IR, if only IR is provided).
  2. A contract hash of any symbol M references. Granularity is the symbol, not the whole imported module: M is not rebuilt because an unused export of a dependency changed.
  3. Compiler, runtime ABI, module ABI, C compiler or flag set (the cache key dimensions).
  4. An inlined body, in optimised mode only: if M's cached link-time product inlined or fused a function from N, and that function's Tier B/C IR hash changed.
  5. Build configuration that affects closed-world decisions: the set of open interfaces or the entry points. (Slice checks are chosen by [yield]/[noyield] in the source, so they are already in the source hash and in the effect summaries; there is no separate build setting to track. The lint level is not a dimension: warnings do not affect generated code.)

Not a reason to recompile M: a change in an imported function's body that leaves its contract hash alone (in incremental mode); a change in an unreferenced export.

Ripple of effect changes (the main risk). If net.Conn.send becomes May where it was Never, every caller's contract and generated code change, and so does every caller's callers when their own summary widens. The ripple is bounded by the call graph, and stops wherever a nopark tag or an already-May function absorbs it. The module compile prints the contract diff so the cause is visible; this is the same visibility the ownership metadata already needs.

docs.title: 7. Cross-module propagation, example
docs.text:
package net      export Conn.recv       Park=May   foreign=nonblocking    hash n1
                export Conn.close      Park=Never                         hash n2

package db       import net.Conn.recv@n1
                export query           Park=May (via net.Conn.recv)       hash d1
                export escape          Park=Never                         hash d2

package app      import db.query@d1, db.escape@d2
                handle()   -> Park=May      (via db.query)   inferred; nothing written
                render()   -> Park=Never

If db is rewritten internally to cache rows and query now sometimes avoids recv, its body changes but not its contract: d1 is unchanged, app is not recompiled. If db.escape is changed so that it logs through a May function, its summary becomes May, d2 changes, and app is recompiled (and render, if it called escape, becomes May too).

 app.handle ---May---> db.query ---May---> net.Conn.recv   (extern parks)
      |                                     ^ summary read from net.smod
      +--Never--> app.render                ^ no net source needed
 db.smod carries only: query: May; its IR (Tier C) is read in optimised link only

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text: Each item gives the alternatives, the trade-off and a recommended direction. A recommendation is not a decision: it is what to build first and test.

docs.title: D1. Where continuation lowering happens
docs.text:
• At module compile. Every function is lowered to the Level-0 convention; the module's C and object are final. Pros: fast incremental builds, no IR needed to link, predictable. Cons: no cross-module frame fusion.
  • At application link. Modules ship IR only; lowering runs on the whole program. Pros: best optimisation. Cons: slow links, requires IR from every dependency, weak caching.
  • Both (recommended). Lower at module compile. In optimised mode, re-lower only chains whose inlining or fusion changes them, using retained Tier C IR.

Recommendation: both, with module compile authoritative. Release a first compiler that does only module-level lowering.

docs.title: D2. Borrowed locals and the lazy shape
docs.text:
The lazy strategy copies locals into a frame only on a park, which moves them. A borrow of a moved local dangles. See suspension.

  • Frame-resident borrowed locals; the function uses eager frames (recommended). Correct; loses the lazy saving for functions with borrowed-across-park locals.
  • Pin the local's storage in the task arena. The local is in the arena from the start, not the stack. Cheaper than a full frame; one more arena operation.
  • Forbid borrowing across a park. Simple; too restrictive (recv(buf&)).

Recommendation: the first, then measure how many hot functions it affects. The toy benchmarks did not include this.

docs.title: D3. The minimum IR for cross-module optimisation
docs.text:
Alternatives: (a) full typed IR for all functions; (b) IR for functions under a size threshold and generic ones only; (c) author-marked inlinable functions only.

Recommendation: ship (b) by default as Tier B plus a size-limited Tier C, with the full IR as an option for libraries that want fusion. Measure size against build gain before deciding the default. Minimum requirements on any IR: explicit ownership operations, call-site effects, park points, cleanup scopes, source-independent.

docs.title: D4. Representing effects in public interfaces
docs.text:
Alternatives: (a) infer everything and export it (current plan); (b) require the author to declare the effect of public functions; (c) infer, and let the author optionally assert it.

(b) reintroduces colouring. (a) alone lets an implementation change ripple silently through dependants. Recommendation: (c) - an optional [nopark] assertion (see suspension 1.1), plus tooling that prints the contract diff between versions, and a version policy that treats widening as breaking. Open: whether the attribute form should also replace the existing parks modifier (extern fn[parks]) and extern blocking (extern fn[blocking]) for consistency, and whether to allow parks on non-extern functions as a "may park" promise for stability.

docs.title: D5. Recursion and dynamic dispatch
docs.text: Recursion: SCC fixed point; per-activation frames; depth-counter fallback to frames on the fast path (see suspension). Dispatch: declared bound, default May. Open: the depth limit, and recursion through interfaces where the bound is the only information. Recommendation as written on those pages; test with a recursive-descent parser handler and a visitor over a tree.

docs.title: D6. Generics: monomorphisation or shared code
docs.text: Monomorphised: exact frames and effects, requires Tier B IR, code growth. Shared with dictionaries: no IR dependence, slower, hard to give generic frames a layout. Recommendation: monomorphise; revisit if code size hurts.

docs.title: D7. Can frame fusion work across separately compiled modules
docs.text: It can only when the callee's IR is present (Tier C) at link time. It cannot at module compile. If the callee's module ships A+B only, fusion simply does not happen across it. Alternative: export a fixed frame layout for chosen functions so callers can embed them without IR. This freezes the layout (breaking ABI to change). Recommendation: fusion at link time from IR only; no fixed layouts. Measure the benefit before building it: the toy numbers suggest about a nanosecond per call.

docs.title: D8. Debugging, stack traces and profiling
docs.text:
A parked task's native stack is gone; the logical stack is the frame chain. Fusion, lazy frames and inlining make logical frames not correspond to physical ones.

  • Park-point tables in every module (recommended): (frame type, state) -> chain of logical frames with source locations, as DWARF-style inline info. Tooling walks the frame chain for parked tasks, and the native stack plus the chain for running ones.
  • Profilers sample the native stack and append the chain. Needs a runtime hook.
  • Alternative: no maps; stack traces show only physical frames. Cheap, poor for diagnosing the "may park" chain which principle 10 demands tooling show.

docs.title: D9. Dynamic module loading and whole-program optimisation
docs.text: Aggressive devirtualisation and fusion assume a closed world; plugins break it. Alternatives: no dynamic loading; open interfaces declared in build configuration; a runtime flag that turns off closed-world assumptions entirely. Recommendation: no dynamic loading in the first compiler; keep bound-based dispatch so it can be added with open interfaces declared in configuration.

docs.title: D10. Blocking FFI
docs.text: Offload pool, dedicated thread, or run on worker. See the table in dispatch. Recommendation: nonblocking where possible; extern blocking offload by default; watchdog diagnostics.

docs.title: D11. Versioning module compatibility and native caches
docs.text: Format, ABI, contract hashes, cache keys as in modules. Open: whether the compatibility policy is enforced by the compiler (refuse a minor-version consumer of a major-breaking producer) or only reported; how long caches live; reproducible builds and cache portability across machines.

docs.title: D12. Cancellation as a non-exception
docs.text: Recommended: not in throws, not catchable, runs cleanups. Alternative: a catchable exception that must be rethrown. Interacts with the exception model (spec 10.7), and with child-vthread scopes.

docs.title: D13. Runaway non-parking code
docs.text:
Decided by the author: the compiler inserts slice checks only in functions marked [yield], or in a type (struct Parser[yield]) or, once packages exist, a package whose default is [yield]. The innermost level wins: function, then type, then package. [noyield] overrides an enclosing default; [nopark] asserts that nothing parks. With no attribute nothing is inserted. Mechanism and rules: suspension 1.1. Loops add no effect by default, so the library-tagging burden an earlier default-on design carried is gone.

The price is that unmarked CPU-bound code can stall a worker and cannot be cancelled. Mitigations, all Direction: loop warnings with an advisory loops class in the module summary (suspension 1.3), a watchdog diagnostic that reports a worker making no progress past a threshold and names the function it is in (it reports and does not interrupt), and the type-level (later package-level) default for CPU-heavy code. Open: the package notion itself, and whether the attribute spelling should be unified between functions and types.

Still open:

  • Overhead of a check in a [yield] loop. Unmeasured; strip-mining and small-bound elision are expected to keep it low. Benchmark B13.
  • Slice unit. An iteration counter (cheap, not time) against a timestamp or a flag set from another thread. Recommendation: counter, sized in iterations per check block; the watchdog flag later.
  • Lambdas inheriting the enclosing function's setting.
  • Default revisited. Whether checks should become the default later, once B13 and a real compiler show the cost and the ripple. The earlier design made them the default and was reversed before any implementation.
  • Interaction with the lazy shape. A check is a park point inside a loop, so the loop's live values must be spillable; a loop with borrowed locals falls under D2 too.

docs.title: D14. Packages and imports
docs.text:
Direction, following the Java folder convention; the details are open. Every sample .stra file starts with package name.

  • Rule used in the samples. A package is a folder. Its name is the folder path under the source root (stra/) with dots for slashes, so stra/redis/ is redis and stra/http/styles/cpp/ is http.styles.cpp. Every file in the folder starts with the same package line, and the compiler rejects a file whose package line does not match its folder. A package compiles to one .smod named after it. Declarations are visible across the files of a package with no import. import other names another package, so import redis.types inside redis is gone and import runtime.leaves became import runtime.
  • Package default. [yield], [noyield] or [nopark] is written on the package line, package[yield] imaging, and repeated on that line in every file of the folder. All files must state the identical line; a file that differs or omits it is an error. There is no special file. Alternatives: the attribute in one file only (hidden action at a distance, and one file becomes special), a package-info-style file (rejected), or in a build manifest (the setting is no longer visible in source). Recommendation: repeat it, since the repetition is a few tokens and keeps the setting visible wherever the code is read. Open: the compiler could instead infer the line from the folder and only require the attribute to be repeated.
  • Style variants. http/styles/{cpp,java,mixed}/server.stra are now separate packages (http.styles.cpp, ...), each of one file, which import http and import runtime. They are alternatives and not compiled together.
  • Import granularity. Whole package (used here), or named symbols (import runtime.Conn). Whole package is simpler; symbol imports give the contract hashes in .smod a natural unit, and they are already per symbol there. Recommendation: whole package at the source level.
  • Visibility. What a package exports to others, and how encapsulated sync code (spec 7.2) is protected from being bypassed. Not specified yet.
  • Nesting. Dots mean folder nesting. Whether a nested package can see its parent's declarations (Java: it cannot) is undecided; recommendation: it cannot.
  • Versions. The .smod carries the package version (modules); how a source tree states which version of an imported package it expects.

docs.title: 1. The may-park effect
docs.text:
Every function has an inferred effect summary. The part that matters for suspension is the park effect:

Park(f) = Never          f cannot park, on any path
        | May            f may park
        | Cond(P)        f parks only if an argument bound to a member of P may park
                         (P = function-typed parameters, interface-typed parameters, type parameters)

with the order Never < Cond(P) < May. The complete summary, which also records throws and foreign blocking, is in modules.

docs.title: Sources of parking
docs.text:
A function's own body can park only through these, and the analysis starts from them:

  1. A call to an extern parks fn (sleep, yield, waitAny, Conn.recv, Conn.send, ...). Already in stra/runtime/leaves.stra.
  2. Entering sync/mutate (it queues FIFO, see spec 7.1). The body of the block can never park, so a lock is never held across a suspension.
  3. A call to a function whose summary is May, or Cond(P) with a member of P bound to something that may park.
  4. A call through an interface or function value whose declared bound permits parking (see dispatch).
  5. A compiler-inserted slice check, only in a function that asks for one with [yield], on the function itself or through its type or package (section 1.1). The check sits on loop back-edges and recursive-call entries of that function's own body; when the slice is exhausted the task yields, which is an ordinary park point. Without [yield] the compiler inserts nothing.
  6. A call to a blocking foreign function that the runtime offloads (see blocking FFI).

Cleanup methods are Never by rule (spec section 9). A cleanup that tries to call a May function is a compile error, which is already the behaviour for sync/mutate bodies.

docs.title: Propagation
docs.text:
The effect propagates transitively over the call graph. Within a module it is computed as a fixed point over strongly connected components of the call graph:

for each SCC in reverse topological order:
    repeat until no change:
        for f in SCC:
            f.park = join(own park sources of f,
                          Park(g) for each direct callee g,    // imported g: read from its summary
                          bound(i) for each indirect call i)   // see dispatch

Mutually recursive functions share one SCC and end up with the same effect. A recursive function with no park source anywhere in its SCC stays Never.

Across modules the same computation runs on summaries (a few words per function) and never needs the callee's code. That is what lets an application be checked without anyone's source.

docs.title: Programmer-facing consequences
docs.text:
• No colouring in source. Waiting (I/O, locks, sleeping) is inferred, never written. This is the one exception to principle 10 ("no hidden behaviour"), and it is unchanged.
  • Nothing is inserted unless the code says so. The compiler adds a yield only inside a function marked [yield]. This keeps principle 10 intact for scheduling: what the code says is what happens.
  • Visibility is tooling's job (Decided, principle 10): hover, lints and errors that name the chain handle -> loadUser -> pool.acquire -> Conn.recv.

docs.title: 1.1 Attributes: [yield], [noyield], [nopark]
docs.text:
Three attributes on a function (fn[yield] name(...)). Spellings are the author's; the rest is Direction.

Attribute Slice checks May wait on I/O or a lock Meaning none none, unless an enclosing type or package says [yield] inferred The default: nothing inserted [yield] inserted in this function's own loops and recursion inferred "The compiler may yield for me here" [noyield] none, even if an enclosing type or package says [yield] inferred Overrides an enclosing default [nopark] none no Assertion: any park source is a compile error. Implies [noyield]
  • Where an attribute can be written, and precedence. The innermost level wins, and the same three attributes work at every level:
Level Written as Applies to Function fn[yield] parse() its own body Type struct Parser[yield] { ... } the methods declared in it Package package[yield] imaging, repeated on the package line of every file in the folder every function in the package Default nothing written nothing inserted

A CPU-heavy type marks itself once and tags its hot, bounded helpers [noyield]. A [nopark] type asserts that none of its methods can park; a method can still override it, and the override is then reported at the method. Files are not a level: a file is a layout accident. - Package. Follows the Java folder convention. A package is a folder, its name is the folder path under the source root with dots for slashes (stra/http/styles/cpp/ is http.styles.cpp), and every file in the folder starts with the same package line. There is no special file. A package default is written on that package line, package[yield] imaging; because the line is repeated in every file, the setting is visible wherever you read, and all files of a package must state the identical line (a file that differs or omits it is an error). The package compiles to one .smod named after it. Placeholder syntax; the rules are in D14. - Resolved at definition. The compiler resolves each function's effective attribute when it compiles the defining package, and the IR carries the resolved value. A generic instantiated in another package keeps the setting of the package that defined it; settings are never inherited by importers. The package default is part of the module's input hash: changing it recompiles the package and its effect changes ripple as usual. - Tooling must show the effective setting and its source (function, type or package) in hover, because it is no longer visible at the function itself. That is the cost of having levels. - Spelling. The attribute follows fn on a function and the name on a type, which differ; whether to unify them (fn f[yield]) is Open. - Own body only. [yield] does not make callees yield. It is shorthand for a yield() every N iterations of the function's own loops. Its callers become May by ordinary inference. - The effect widens only if a check is inserted. A [yield] function with no loop or recursion stays Never; tagging it causes no ripple. - What a check is: a counter decrement and a rarely taken branch. The counter is the task's slice: the amount of work (a count of loop iterations) it may do before it must give the worker up. It is the time slice of a scheduler, and has nothing to do with array slices such as buf[..n]. On exhaustion the task goes to the back of the run queue and resumes in its turn: a park point, so live values are spilled to a frame as for any park. A check is also a cancellation point, so a task in a [yield] loop can be cancelled (section 4). - Cost control (Direction): strip-mine loops so the counter is tested once per block of iterations; omit the check for loops with a small constant bound. Neither is guaranteed. The overhead is a measurement to take, not assume (benchmarks B13). - [nopark] is the strict form. It is the only form that guarantees the function is Never. [noyield] still permits a call to recv. It is an optional assertion, never required, and never mentioned by callers; it turns a silent effect change into a compile error at a library boundary. - Lambdas inherit the setting of the enclosing function (Open). - [yield] is not the yield() call. yield() is an extern parks fn the program calls itself. The attribute only lets the compiler insert yields. - Limits: the slice bounds how long a checked region runs. It does not bound a function without [yield], a plain extern fn, or a single indivisible library operation. Such code stalls its worker and cannot be cancelled until it returns. The loop warnings in 1.3 exist to find it.

docs.title: 1.2 Calls allowed in sync/mutate bodies, cleanups and C callbacks
docs.text:
These regions may not park, so they may call only functions whose effect is Never.

Allowed:

  • A function inferred Never: no park source anywhere below it. Looping helpers qualify, since without [yield] loops add no effect.
  • A function tagged [nopark].
  • A Cond(P) function whose arguments are statically non-parking.
  • A plain extern fn (a promise of a short, non-blocking call; unverifiable).
  • Operations that do not park: new, field access, throw, Ref copies.

Rejected, with the call chain in the message:

  • Any May function. That includes one that is May only because it is marked [yield] and has a loop.
  • Anything that parks: sleep, recv, send, yield().
  • Entering another sync/mutate, unless that object is in the same head.
  • A call through an interface or function value whose declared bound is not Never (the default bound is May).

Inside such a region a [yield] marking is ignored for the region's own loops: no check is inserted there, and a type- or package-level [yield] does not apply.

Why a body may not park (the rule is a design choice, not a technical limit; frames could hold a lock):

  1. Hold time stays bounded by the code in the block. A holder parked on a socket keeps the lock while every other vthread queues; with FIFO fairness one waiting writer also blocks the readers behind it.
  2. Two vthreads on one worker never contend. A body that cannot park runs to completion before anything else runs on that worker, so contention is only across workers, where the runtime can spin briefly before parking. That spin removed a 55 to 75 percent throughput loss (bench/results/miniredis.md).
  3. Multi-object blocks retry safely. mutate(a, b) takes all its locks before the body runs, or none, and backs off if one is busy. This is safe only because no body code has run. It is also why nested acquisition is an error.
  4. No frame ever owns a lock. Cancellation, errors and unwinding never have to release a lock on behalf of a suspended task.
  5. A class of deadlocks cannot be written: a holder waiting for something that another vthread can provide only after taking the same lock.

What it costs: no I/O under a lock (copy out, release, then act, as Db.get and Db.set do), and long work under a lock must be chunked (purgeExpired removes at most PURGE_BATCH keys per hold).

docs.title: 1.3 Loop warnings
docs.text:
A lint, not a proof. Termination is undecidable, so these are warnings and never errors.

Classification. Each loop gets a class, and each function gets a loops class in its summary, composed over its callees by the same rules as nested loops. The class describes uninterrupted work: a loop whose body contains a park point (a call to any May function, a [yield] check, yield(), a lock entry) contributes none, because every iteration gives the scheduler a chance. purgeExpired in stra/redis/db.stra is the example: its outer loop yields, and the inner loop under the lock is bounded by a counter against a constant.

loops Meaning none No loop or recursion bounded Every loop advances a counter or iterator toward a constant bound under the threshold long A constant bound above the threshold; a bound that is loop-invariant but not constant (a configured limit such as lim.maxBulk); iteration over a collection of unstated size; or nested loops whose product exceeds the threshold unbounded No proven progress toward an exit: loop {}, a while where nothing moves the condition, or unbounded recursion

A loop that advances a counter toward a loop-invariant bound terminates even when the bound is only known at run time, so the compiler can see it without any annotation. A stated limit that the program enforces with an ordinary if/throw (principle 11) is visible the same way.

Calls through interfaces, function values and foreign code contribute nothing at normal levels (a lint is not a proof) and are listed as unknown at the strictest level.

What warns. Within [noyield], [nopark] and sync/mutate bodies:

  • unbounded own loop or recursion;
  • a call to a function whose summary says unbounded (the chain is printed: tight -> parse -> scanForever);
  • long, at the stricter levels.

When it runs. Off by default in ordinary builds, except for one case: unbounded inside a sync/mutate body always warns, because spec 7.1 relies on hold time being bounded by the block, and nothing else enforces it. A flag selects levels (placeholder --warn-loops=off|marked|reachable|all): marked covers [noyield] and [nopark] functions; reachable adds unmarked functions reachable from spawn roots; all adds everything. Editor and CI use it freely.

Suppression. An allow-attribute on the function or loop (placeholder). It acknowledges the warning and makes no claim about the loop.
