A loop-level bound annotation was considered and dropped: if the compiler can see a counter or constant it is redundant, if not it is an unchecked claim, yielding at the bound is just [yield], and silently stopping at the bound hides behaviour. The only coherent form is an ordinary if/throw on a limit, which the program can already write.

What the module exposes. The loops class is part of each exported function's summary, in a separate advisory section that is not part of the contract hash, so a change in loop structure never forces dependants to recompile. A caller's lint reads the callee's current .smod, and the warning can lag until relink (modules).

Known limits. It will miss unbounded work inside loops that look bounded, flag some bounded loops it cannot prove bounded, and sees foreign and indirect calls only as stated.

docs.title: Example: attributes, sync and loop warnings
docs.text:
Illustrative Strata source and C. Neither is compiler output.

// http/headers.stra
package http

// Opted in: the compiler inserts a slice check in this loop. May, yields only.
fn[yield] parseHeaders(buf: u8[]&): Headers throws BadRequest {
    var h = Headers();
    var i = 0;
    while i < buf.len {              // back-edge: slice check inserted here
        let line = nextLine(buf, i);
        h.add(line);
        i = line.end;
    }
    return h;
}

// No attribute: nothing inserted. No loop effect, so Never: usable under a lock.
fn hash(key: u8[]&): u64 {
    var x: u64 = 14695981039346656037;
    for b in key { x = (x ^ b) * 1099511628211; }
    return x;
}

fn lookup(cache: Ref<Cache>, key: u8[]&): i64? {
    let h = hash(key);               // Never: fine
    sync(cache) {                    // the body may call only Never functions
        return cache.entries.get(h); // get() is Never unless it is [yield] or parks
    }
}

fn[nopark] broken(k: u8[]&) {
    sleep(1ms);                      // error: park source in a nopark function
                                     //   broken -> sleep (extern parks)
}

fn[nopark] spin(flag: Flag&) {
    while !flag.isSet() { }          // warning (loops): unbounded loop in a nopark function
}

fn tight(cache: Ref<Cache>, r: Reader&) {
    mutate(cache) {
        scanForever(r);              // warning (always on in a lock body): scanForever loops unbounded
    }                                //   tight -> scanForever
}

The three levels together. The folder is the package; each file repeats the package line:

imaging/
    renderer.stra
    metrics.stra

// imaging/renderer.stra
package[yield] imaging                    // package default: functions here get slice checks

struct Renderer {                         // no attribute: inherits [yield] from the package
    fn render(page: Page&): string { for b in page.blocks { ... } }   // gets checks
    fn[noyield] crc(data: u8[]&): u32 { ... }                          // the function overrides: plain C
}

// imaging/metrics.stra
package[yield] imaging                    // the same line as in renderer.stra

struct Metrics[noyield] {                 // the type overrides the package default
    fn width(c: u32): u32 { return c < 128 ? 1 : 2 }                  // no checks (the type says noyield)
    fn[yield] widest(text: string&): u32 { for c in text { ... } }    // the function overrides the type
}

fn[nopark] isAscii(c: u32): bool { return c < 128 }                   // asserts it never parks

Inferred effects and summary fields:

hash          Never   loops=bounded   (no attribute, no checks)
nextLine      Never   loops=none
parseHeaders  May     yields=true  loops=long
lookup        May     (acquiring the lock can park)
spin          Never   loops=unbounded (nopark, warns)

C for parseHeaders:

st_t parseHeaders_call(task_t *t, u8buf *buf, Headers *out) {
    Headers h = headers_new();
    size_t i = 0;
    while (i < buf->len) {
        if (--t->worker->slice <= 0) {              // slice check
            // a yield is a real park: spill live values into a frame
            parse_frame *f = frame_new(t, parseHeaders_resume, /*state*/ 1);
            f->buf = buf; f->h = h; f->i = i;        // buf is a borrowed parameter, see D2
            run_queue_push_back(t);
            return PARKED;
        }
        Line line = nextLine(buf, i);                // plain call
        headers_add(&h, line);
        i = line.end;
    }
    *out = h;
    return DONE;
}
// parseHeaders_resume re-enters the loop with f->h and f->i restored, or on CANCELLED
// runs the cleanups for h, frees the frame and returns CANCELLED.
  • hash has no counter and no status, so the C compiler can inline it freely.
  • On the common path a check costs a decrement and a branch per iteration. Strip-mining would test once per block. Neither cost nor strip-mining is measured yet (B13).
  • If buf pointed at a native-stack local in the caller, the caller would need a frame-resident local, or the yield would leave a dangling borrow (D2).

docs.title: The three shapes of a function
docs.text:
Park(f) Generated form Never An ordinary C function. No frame, no status codes beyond throws. Cond(P) Compiled as two entries. A call whose P arguments are Never binds to the plain form; otherwise to the suspendable form. May The suspendable form below.

The key property for performance, and the reason conservatism is affordable: a May function that does not park on a given call costs about the same as an ordinary call. This was measured on the hand-written C (bench/results/lazy.md): about 0.7 to 1.5 ns per extra parking call in a chain, against ordinary calls, and 3.4 ns for the whole four-deep request. It is a microbenchmark with hot frames, so it supports "conservative contracts are cheap enough to be the default" and not much more.

docs.title: The suspendable form: native-stack fast path, frames made on demand (Direction)
docs.text:
Each May function is compiled to a pair:

f_call(task, args..., out*) -> status       runs on the worker's native stack
f_resume(task, frame*)      -> status       state-machine entry used after a park

status = DONE | THROWN | PARKED

f_call is the function as written, as straight C. Calls to other May functions check the returned status. If the callee returns PARKED, f_call does not park by itself. It allocates a frame, copies out the locals that are live across that call, records its state number, links the frame to the callee's frame, and returns PARKED to its own caller. The next function up does the same. A chain of N frames is therefore built from the leaf upward, during one return, and only when the park really happens.

When the event arrives, the scheduler calls the innermost frame's f_resume. When that finishes, it resumes its parent frame directly, in turn. This is the lazy strategy plus direct resume from the experiments. Two measured reasons it is the first choice:

  • Parks are rare relative to calls in typical handlers, so the common path allocates nothing (lazy.md: allocations per request = p x (D+1)).
  • Resuming only the innermost frame, rather than re-entering every frame from the root as Rust async does, kept wake cost flat with depth: 6.3 ns against 26.2 ns at depth 16 (bench/results/frames.txt).

The alternatives stay on the table because lazy needs two code versions per function that must agree on state numbering, and was 1.2x the code size of eager in the toy:

Strategy Allocations when no park Code When it wins Eager: a frame per May call D+1 smallest Frame-resident locals (below); debug builds Embedded: callee frames inside caller's frame 0 or 1 per task medium Chains that nearly always park (p near 1) Lazy: frames made while unwinding p x (D+1) largest Rare parks; default

The compiler may choose per function (Direction). The choice is invisible to callers because they only see status; that is what makes it a module-level decision and not an ABI one.

docs.title: Frame layout
docs.text:
A frame is:

+------------------------------+
| resume function pointer      |   header, identical for every function
| state number                 |   (the stable part of the ABI)
| parent frame link            |
| task pointer                 |
| result/out slot binding      |
+------------------------------+
| live slots                   |   private to the function
+------------------------------+

Live slots are the values live at some suspension point. Slots that are never live at the same time share storage, by the usual register-colouring over park points. Temporaries live across a park (an argument already evaluated for a call that has not happened, a pending Ref promotion) are slots like any others.

Frames come from a per-function arena, sized exactly. This matches the existing per-type arena rule and the frames_bench model; idle parked task cost there was 137 B with no state and 393 B at depth 4, against a 4 KB floor for a stackful fiber (Measured, hand-written).

Frames never move (Direction). A frame address is stable from creation to destruction. This removes the Pin problem Rust async has, and lets other code hold pointers into a frame.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
// db/query.stra
package db                                  // compiled separately         Park(query) = May   (calls Conn.recv)
fn query(sql: string&, id: i64): Row throws DbError {
    let c = pool.acquire();                 // May: waits for a free connection
    c.send(encode(sql, id));                // May
    return decode(c.recv());                // May
}

// app/handle.stra
package app
import db
fn handle(req: Request&): Response throws DbError {
    let row = db.query("select ...", req.id);   // inferred May; nothing written
    return render(row);                         // Never
}

Generated C for handle (illustrative; names and layout are not fixed):

typedef struct { frame_hdr h; Request *req; } handle_frame;   // row is not live across a park, so not a slot

st_t app_handle_call(task_t *t, Request *req, Response *out) {
    Row row;
    st_t s = db_query_call(t, "select ...", req->id, &row);
    if (s == PARKED) {                              // a real park, happening now
        handle_frame *f = frame_new(t, app_handle_resume, /*state*/ 1);
        f->req = req;
        t->innermost->parent = f;                   // link callee's frame to ours
        t->innermost->out = &f->h.result;           // the result now lands in the frame, not on our stack
        return PARKED;
    }
    if (s == THROWN) return THROWN;                 // no cleanups pending in this function
    *out = render(&row);                            // Never: a plain call
    return DONE;
}

st_t app_handle_resume(task_t *t, handle_frame *f) {
    switch (f->h.state) {
    case 1: {                                       // db.query finished
        if (t->wake == THROWN) { frame_free(f); return THROWN; }
        Response r = render((Row *)&f->h.result);
        frame_free(f);
        return finish(t, &r);                       // resume parent directly or complete the task
    }}
}

One real hazard shows in t->innermost->out = ...: the callee was given a pointer into the caller's native stack. Pointers to locals that are live across a park are the subject of the next subsection.

docs.title: Borrows and locals that cannot be moved
docs.text:
The lazy form copies locals into a frame only when a park occurs. A copy changes the address. Two things can hold the old address:

  1. A borrow (T&) to a local, given to a callee that is part of the park chain, or kept in another local.
  2. A result or out pointer (above), which the unwinding step can rebind because it is compiler-generated.

Case 2 is mechanical. Case 1 is not: let buf = readBuffer(); conn.recv(buf&) is exactly this shape, and extremely common.

Direction: a local that is borrowed and live across a call that may park is frame-resident from its declaration, in a frame created at function entry. A function with any frame-resident local uses the eager shape for that function. Other functions in the chain stay lazy. The borrow-origin analysis (spec section 5) already has what is needed to decide this; the new fact is only that the flag borrowed across a may-park call is recorded for each local. This is a real constraint on how often lazy applies, and not measured: the toy benchmark has no borrowed locals. See open decision D2.

docs.title: 3. Calls that never suspend
docs.text:
Never functions compile to ordinary C and are inlined by the C compiler under its usual rules. Without [yield], a loop adds no effect, so most helpers (parsing, rendering, hashing) are Never. A Cond(P) function called with a known non-parking argument binds to its plain entry.

For a May function the non-suspending path should be straight-line C with one status test after each May call. The cost of that test is what the 0.7 to 1.5 ns above measures.

docs.title: Errors (throws)
docs.text:
C has no unwinding, so a throw is a status return (THROWN) with the exception in the task, and each function branches to its cleanup block for the scope it is in, then returns THROWN. This is the same machinery as the park return, which is why the two compose. Not built in the C prototypes yet (listed in open-questions.md).

Across a park, a thrown exception arriving at f_resume (t->wake == THROWN) enters the same cleanup blocks as it would on the fast path. The cleanup code is shared between f_call and f_resume; this is a code generation requirement, not a runtime one.

docs.title: Cancellation (Direction)
docs.text:
Cooperative, as in spec 6.2: the cancelling party marks the task and wakes it. A task is only ever cancelled at a park point, because that is where its state is in a frame. The wake carries wake = CANCELLED, and f_resume takes the unwinding path: run cleanups of the scopes it is in, free its own frame, resume the parent with CANCELLED, and so on up the chain. Frames are never discarded without running cleanups, and cleanups never park, so unwinding is bounded.

Cancellation is not an ordinary exception: it is not named in throws, and catch cannot swallow it. Letting catch (Exception) swallow it would make cancellation unreliable; requiring it in throws would put the effect back in signatures everywhere. This choice interacts with the open exception-model question (spec 10.7) and is stated here as Direction only.

A task can be cancelled at any park point, including a slice check, so a task spinning in a [yield] loop is cancellable. A task in a loop without [yield], a nopark function, a plain extern fn or an indivisible library operation is not, until it returns.

docs.title: Deterministic cleanup
docs.text: Cleanup of a resource runs when its scope exits, by normal return, THROWN or CANCELLED, and happens before the frame is freed. Task-level cleanup precedes reclamation of any task arena (spec section 9, unchanged). A parked task holding a sync permission is impossible by construction (no park inside the block), so no frame ever owns a lock.

docs.title: 5. Recursion
docs.text:
• A recursive function with park sources in its SCC is May. Each activation has its own frame, taken from an arena, so recursion depth while parked is limited by memory, not by a stack size.
  • On the fast path a recursive May function consumes native stack until it returns or parks. A runaway recursion that never parks would overflow the worker's stack, as in any C program. Direction: a depth counter in recursive May functions; past a limit they switch to the eager shape (frames, not native stack), so depth is bounded by the declared limits (principle 11) rather than by the worker stack. Open: the limit, and whether recursive Never functions also need a declared depth bound.
  • Mutual recursion across modules is not possible through ordinary imports (module imports form a DAG). It can occur through interface calls, where the effect is the declared bound (see dispatch).

docs.title: 6. Interaction with ownership
docs.text: Concern Rule (Direction unless stated) Ref<T> live across a park Held in a frame slot; the slot is an owner. Frame destruction (normal, thrown or cancelled) releases it. A parked task therefore keeps its objects alive. WeakRef<T> live across a park Held in a slot. Promotion is a separate step after the resume, as everywhere (spec 3.1). The compiler must not hoist a promotion across a park point: the object may have expired meanwhile. Borrow T& live across a park Allowed if the referent outlives the parked task. The lifetime analysis (spec section 5) already tracks origins; the new check is that every referent a borrow can point to is either frame-resident, a Ref held by the frame, or static. A borrow of a native-stack local is the case handled above. Task temporary arena Belongs to the vthread, not to a frame. Survives parks. Reclaimed at task exit after cleanups. Per-function frame arenas Runtime-owned like per-type arenas. A frame can be freed on a different worker from the one that allocated it (a task can resume anywhere once migration exists), so frees must be cross-thread-safe; the same requirement as new. Escape analysis (spec 4.4) A value that does not escape the task may live in the task arena or in a frame slot. The compiler must preserve destructor timing across parks.

docs.title: 7. Optimisation opportunities
docs.text:
These are not guaranteed. Each is something the compiler may do when conditions hold, and none changes behaviour. The tier column says what each needs from the module format.

Opportunity What it is Conditions Needs Frame embedding The callee's slots live inside the caller's frame. One allocation per task instead of D+1. Callee frame size known; callee not recursive; one live activation per caller activation. Callee layout (link time, or a fixed layout exported from its module) Allocation elimination No frame for a function that never parks in practice Not provable; use lazy instead, which allocates only on a park None State-machine fusion Inline a May callee into its caller so its park points become states of the caller's machine; one frame, one resume function. Single call site, or small callee; direct (not virtual) target; not recursive. Callee IR (Tier C) Flattening A chain a -> b -> c becomes one machine The same, repeated; code size bounded Callee IR Slot overlay Slots from inlined callees share storage by liveness After fusion IR Direct resume Resume the innermost frame only Always applied by the lazy/direct scheme None Park-free specialisation A Cond(P) function called with a non-parking argument becomes Never Argument's effect known statically Summary

Limits on fusion: code size growth; an exported function still needs its own standalone entry points; debugging and profiling need a map from fused states back to logical frames (see open decisions D8); cancellation points and cleanup scopes of the inlined function must keep their order and timing exactly; recursion and virtual calls block it. The measured upper bound on what any of this can save is small in the toy case: about 1 ns per parking call, "a request that does any real work costs thousands of times more" (lazy.md). Fusion is therefore a later, evidence-driven optimisation, not part of the first compiler.

docs.title: 8. Relative to Java virtual threads and Rust async
docs.text:
Aspect Java virtual threads Rust async Strata (Direction) Source Plain blocking style async fn, .await, runtime choice Plain blocking style Suspension visible in signatures No Yes (async) No in source; yes in tooling and module summaries Implementation Stack of a continuation copied to and from the heap by the JVM (stackful) One compiler-generated state machine per async body, composed into a larger one Per-function resumable frames; compiler-generated Memory per parked task Depends on the stack depth at park, copied Size of the composed state machine, known statically Frames per function on the chain; exact, not yet measured in a compiler Can suspend through native frames Pinned or blocked in some cases (native, and synchronized on older JDKs) Not applicable: await only crosses async code No: foreign frames cannot be captured, so the rules in dispatch apply Runtime requirement JVM with JIT and GC Library executor Small C runtime, no GC, no JIT Dynamic code and reflection Natural Limited Weaker; closed-world assumptions help the optimiser Recursion Natural Needs boxing Natural (frames from arenas) dyn / virtual Natural Needs Box<dyn Future> and Pin Uniform: effect bound in the interface Cost of a function that might park but does not A call A poll, plus the state machine's size A call plus a status test (Measured, toy)

Advantages Strata is aiming for: no function colouring and no Pin; precise frames with no stack copying; deterministic cleanup on cancellation (Rust async cancels by dropping, Java by interrupts); no runtime beyond the C one.

Trade-offs and limitations, stated plainly:

  • Every function the analysis marks May costs a status test per May call and extra generated code. The analysis can mark a function May because of a deep, unseen callee; nothing in the source says so.
  • Compile-time complexity moves from the programmer to the compiler: effect inference, frame layout, two code versions per function, and a module format that must carry it all.
  • Foreign code cannot be suspended in the middle. Java's pinning problem exists here in a different form (see dispatch).
  • Stack traces and profilers see the native stack, not the logical one, unless the toolchain supplies maps.
  • No performance superiority is claimed. The existing measurements are small, hand-written, and mostly show a memory advantage over stackful fibers (and parity with Tokio-class frames). See the evaluation plan.

docs.title: 9. Where stackful execution remains
docs.text:
1. As the reference semantics. The tests that decide whether a language feature is correct should pass under both implementations, which is cheap to arrange if the stackful runtime is kept working.
  2. As a baseline for the evaluation plan: stackful fibers are the cost to beat on memory (4 KB floor, 4.1 KB resident at 1 KB state against Tokio's 1.4 KB).
  3. For synchronous drivers on blocking-pool threads, where a foreign callback needs to call parking Strata code (dispatch).

It is no longer the primary implementation path. Spec section 6.1 is rewritten accordingly.

docs.title: The journey
docs.text:
Step Question Answer in one line 1. Why Strata What does Goose leave out for servers? Dynamic objects, shared state and many lightweight threads. 2. Foundations What do fibers, arenas, refcounts and frames cost? A 4 KB fiber floor, free arena layout choices, no biased counts, about 1 ns per parking call. 3. An HTTP server Can the model carry a real server? Yes: 88 to 94 B per idle connection, throughput syscall-bound. 4. Rust and Go Is it any better than what exists? Memory per connection, yes; pipelined throughput, about 2x; real handlers shrink the gap. 5. mini-redis What does a second, different server break? Cross-worker wakeups, pub/sub backpressure, a shared database. 6. Locks that park How should sync and mutate wait? Park in FIFO order, spin briefly first, acquire several locks all-or-nothing.

All numbers were measured on one machine (Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Linux 6.12, gcc 14.2, rustc 1.93, Go 1.24, OpenJDK 25), usually from single runs. Raw data lives in bench/results/.

docs.title: 1. Why Strata
docs.text:
Goose offers compiler-managed lifetimes, native C output and large virtual-memory reservations that let selected arrays grow in place. Its strict thread isolation and limited dynamic allocation make typical server programs awkward.

Strata keeps those ideas and adds what a server needs:

  • dynamically created objects and graphs with independent lifetimes
  • thousands of virtual threads running ordinary sequential code
  • efficient shared, read-heavy state such as caches
  • deterministic cleanup of files, sockets and locks
  • reference safety without writing lifetime names like 'a

It is not a Goose fork or a Rust dialect, and it does not try for feature parity with Rust. Understandable semantics win over zero overhead at all costs.

docs.title: The first rules
docs.text:
Two rules shaped everything after them, and both came from the user rather than from measurement:

Principle 10: no hidden magic

Aside from virtual threads and parking, nothing happens behind the programmer's back. No implicit buffering, no implicit batching. A library may offer batching, but only when the program asks for it, and it is off by default.

Principle 11: every unbounded input has a limit

A header block, a request body and a parsed document's depth all have limits stated by the program. Big payloads are streamed or spooled to a file, never parsed whole. Exceeding a limit is an error the caller can see.

docs.title: 2. Measuring the foundations
docs.text: Before writing any Strata, the expensive questions got small C benchmarks, compared with Rust (Tokio, slab) and Java virtual threads where one existed. Full tables: group1.md, group2.md, group56.md, lazy.md.

docs.title: Fibers and stacks
docs.text:
Unit (100k idle, 1 KB state) Resident bytes each Tokio task 1,419 (395 with no state) Strata pooled-stack fiber 4,113 (one page floor) Java virtual thread about 809 heap with no state
  • A stackful fiber has a 4 KB floor; a stackless task is about 10x smaller when idle state is small. The gap closes near page size.
  • MADV_NOHUGEPAGE is mandatory with transparent huge pages on: without it a 64 KB stack costs 65 KB resident, and a 1 MB stack almost 1 MB.
  • Per-stack guard pages do not scale: each costs two mappings, and 1M fibers hit the map-count limit.
  • Switching is cheap: about 13 ns with 1k fibers, 35 to 39 ns with 100k.

docs.title: Typed arenas
docs.text:
• Layout (one reservation, a chunk table, or munmap) makes no measurable difference to allocation cost; choose by what handles need.
  • Smaller chunks reclaim better, and geometric growth removes the small-type floor.
  • Against glibc, after freeing everything an arena returns memory (0.3 MB retained against 153 MB).
  • MADV_DONTNEED zero-fills, so a generation stored in a slot is lost when a chunk is decommitted. The fix is a per-chunk epoch kept in the resident chunk header.
  • Long-lived objects scattered through shared chunks pin memory. That is solved by lifetime segregation, which per-type arenas give by construction.

docs.title: Reference counts across threads
docs.text:
• Biased counting is 2 to 7x cheaper than atomic for thread-private objects, but once objects cross threads it is equal or worse (0.71 to 0.87x at 16 threads with message passing).
  • Decision: no biased counting in v1. Types proven thread-confined get plain counts; shared types get plain atomic counts.
  • Messaging stays for passing data, with typed per-vthread mailboxes. Shared memory with sync and mutate is the primary sharing model.

docs.title: Frames for parked calls
docs.text:
Four strategies were compared: plain calls, a heap frame per call (eager), frames embedded in the caller, and lazy frames created only while unwinding a real park.

  • Lazy beats eager by 3.6 ns per request at depth 4 and 7.7 ns at depth 8 when parks are rare. The whole difference between strategies is about 1 ns per parking call.
  • An earlier estimate of 20 to 30 ns saved per request was too high; the measured saving is 4 to 8 ns.
  • Parked memory is the same for lazy and eager.

docs.title: 3. An HTTP server
docs.text: The first proving ground. The server is written as .stra source, with a hand-written C counterpart standing in for compiler output. Tests pin the two together.

docs.title: What it showed
docs.text:
4 workers, 64 active connections per idle connection requests/s Strata-style C, 100k connections 89 B 1.29M Tokio, lazy futures 897 B 1.25M Tokio, naive handler 3,074 B 1.25M
  • The 88 B is sizeof(ConnTask) and nothing else: an idle connection holds no buffer.
  • Throughput is nearly equal because the workload is syscall-bound (about 3 microseconds per request). The frame model buys memory, not a large throughput win.
  • Kernel memory (3 to 3.6 KB per socket) dwarfs all of it and is the same for every server.

docs.title: Features that were added, each from a review
docs.text:
• Size-class input buffers replaced a fixed 2 KB buffer; the reader no longer moves bytes per request.
  • Two body readers: a small in-memory one for APIs (1 MB default) and a file-backed upload reader with a much larger limit. Both refuse an oversize body with 413 before holding it.
  • Pipelined requests run as one child task each, answered in request order, with a barrier for unsafe methods.
  • Opt-in response batching, off by default, with a bound on held responses and a max hold time. It exists to honour principle 10.
  • Lingering close, so an error response is not destroyed by a reset when the client is still sending.
  • Layering: generic support moved into runtime and library files; server.stra holds only the server.

docs.title: Negative controls
docs.text: Each important property has a build that breaks it on purpose (responses in completion order, no body limits, no yield, and so on), and the matching test must fail. 38 tests pass and every control fails as intended.

docs.title: 4. Against Rust and Go
docs.text:
The same design was written in Rust (Tokio) and Go (a pipelined server, and plain net/http), driven by the same tests and load generator.

Pipelined, 1 worker requests/s Strata-style C 4.05M Rust (Tokio) 2.1M Go 2.12M Idle memory per connection bytes Strata-style C 89 to 192 Rust about 1,400 Go 4,000 to 5,000 Go net/http 33,000

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
Caveats

Real handlers do real work, which shrinks the throughput gap a lot. What survives is memory per connection, in-connection concurrency, the timer floor and Go's garbage-collection tail. All runs are single runs on loopback.

Browsers do not pipeline HTTP/1.1 (they multiplex over HTTP/2), so the pipelined number says more about the runtime's cost per request than about web traffic.

docs.title: 5. mini-redis
docs.text:
The second proving ground, chosen because it differs from HTTP: long-lived connections, pub/sub fan-out and one shared database. The server side of tokio-rs/mini-redis was converted (frame, parse, connection, db, server, shutdown, commands).

Conversion depends on no third-party crates

If a program needs a crate, Strata would have no equivalent. The README maps each crate used by the original to a replacement, and lists the standard-library pieces the Strata source assumes.

docs.title: What was new
docs.text:
• Cross-worker wakeups: a publish on one worker must wake a subscriber parked on another.
  • Backpressure: one mailbox per subscriber connection with a declared capacity and an explicit lag policy, Disconnect (default) or Notice.
  • A reaper: cleanup() cannot take a lock, so a dying subscriber hands its subscriptions to a queue, and a purge vthread unsubscribes them.
  • Fairness: a pipelining publisher starved subscribers until each connection yielded every 64 commands.
  • Limits everywhere: frame size, bulk size, key length, key count, topics, subscriptions and queue depth.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Item Result GET/SET 90/10, 1 worker 328k ops/s unpipelined, 468k pipelined 16 deep 4 workers 1.10M to 1.94M; the load generator tops out near 1.3M unpipelined Pub/sub deliveries, 1 / 4 workers 440 to 456k/s / up to 1.98M/s Median delivery latency, 1 worker 12 µs for 1 subscriber, 84 µs for 64, 1.4 ms for 1,000 Idle connection / idle subscriber 297 B / 354 to 594 B

The idle subscriber first cost 4.5 KB because the mailbox ring was allocated at full size; growing it on demand fixed that.

docs.title: Tests and honesty
docs.text:
27 tests pass on six builds (plain, park-only, and both under AddressSanitizer and ThreadSanitizer), with four negative controls. Bugs found along the way included a wake sent to an uninitialised worker and two data races, fixed.

There is no baseline: building the original Rust server was blocked by the permission system, so none of these numbers is compared with Rust.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Entering sync or mutate may park the virtual thread. A holder never parks inside the block (a compile error), so two vthreads on one worker never contend and hold time is bounded by the code in the block.

Several objects in one head, as in mutate(a, b), are acquired all-or-nothing in a fixed global order; if one is busy the acquirer releases everything, parks on that lock's FIFO queue and retries, keeping its arrival ticket. Nested acquisition of another object, reentrancy and read-to-write upgrade are errors.

docs.title: The ordering key
docs.text: The order is by the address of each object's lock word, or (arena id, slot index) for arena objects whose storage can move. A per-allocation sequence number was rejected for its cost. Arenas never compact, and a chunk is freed only when empty, so a live object's address never changes. Only types that appear in a sync or mutate head carry a lock word.

docs.title: The measurement that changed the contract's implementation
docs.text:
With FIFO fairness, one waiting writer makes every later reader queue behind it, and each handoff is a cross-thread wake. Throughput at 4 workers, one lock, 64 connections:

GET share park only spin then park 100% 1.29M 1.29M 90% 570k 1.28M 50% 330k 1.27M 0% 318k 1.27M

A 10% write mix lost 55% of throughput. Spinning 2000 rounds before parking removed the loss. The contract is unchanged (entering still "may park"); only the cost differs. A 100-round spin was noisy, from 1.0M to 326k at 50% reads.

The park-only build remains in the test suite so the handoff path stays covered.

Not yet implemented

The multi-object retry exists only as design. mini-redis has a single lock.
